one_liner: C99 Adaptive Radix Tree: ordered byte-key map/set, algorithmically faster than red-black trees (std::map's structure).
what_it_does: libart is a C99 implementation of the Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), an ordered associative structure keyed on binary-comparable byte strings, supporting insert/search/delete, min/max lookup, full ordered iteration, and prefix-based iteration. It is not a drop-in for std::map: the API is a flat set of C functions (art_insert, art_search, art_delete, art_iter, art_iter_prefix) taking a raw key buffer + length and an opaque void* value, with no templates, iterators, or operator overloads.
how_it_is_fast: ART uses four node types (4/16/48/256 children) sized to actual local fanout instead of one fixed node shape, so small nodes stay cache-small and dense nodes get direct/O(1) child lookup. Path compression (inline partial keys up to MAX_PREFIX_LEN=10 bytes) and lazy expansion collapse single-child chains, bounding worst-case overhead to about 52 bytes/key. On x86/x86-64, Node16's 16-way key comparison is vectorized with SSE2 (_mm_cmpeq_epi8 + movemask + ctz) instead of a scalar loop; other architectures fall back to a plain scan.
when_to_use: Ordered map/set semantics (min/max, ordered iteration, prefix iteration) over keys you can encode as binary-comparable byte strings
Read-heavy, single-threaded in-process indexes (e.g. routing tables, in-memory dictionaries) where you own the key encoding
Key sets where no key is a byte-for-byte prefix of another key, or you pre-length-prefix/terminate keys to avoid that case
x86/x86-64 targets, where the SSE2 Node16 fast path applies (other archs still work via scalar fallback, just without that speedup)
You're willing to vendor and maintain the ~2-file source yourself since the project is unmaintained
when_not_to_use: Any key can be a strict byte-for-byte prefix of another key: issue #56 (open) documents out-of-bounds reads / incorrect leaf-splitting in recursive_insert for exactly this case, with no released fix

Multi-threaded concurrent access: no locks, atomics, or volatile-qualified state in the source; maintainer-adjacent discussion in issue #53 confirms it is not thread-safe and points to forks (e.g. ARTSynchronized) for concurrent variants
You need a drop-in std::map/std::set replacement: this is an untemplated C library with a byte-key/void*-value function API, not a C++ generic container

You need it actively maintained: last commit 2021-02-11, with confirmed bugs (#54 search returns null for prefix+NUL keys, #42 key_len issues, #35 crash in recursive_insert, #17 valgrind warning on prefix keys) still open

You need project-specific speed evidence: libart ships no benchmarks of its own (repo has only src/ and tests/); every claimed number comes from the ART paper's own unreleased implementations, not this codebase

integration.dependencies: none (libcheck is only needed to build the test_runner test suite, not the library)
integration.min_toolchain: C99; comments in art.c work around GCC 4.2.2's broken C99 inline support and a GCC 5.1 loop-unrolling bug, but no explicit minimum compiler version is stated
integration.platforms: any (portable C99); SSE2 fast path compiled only under __i386__/__amd64__ for Node16 child lookup, scalar fallback loop used elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: not thread-safe / not documented as safe — no mutexes, atomics, or volatile-qualified fields in the source; see issue #53
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same broad job as std::map/std::set (ordered key-value lookup) but a different C API (byte-buffer keys, void* values, callback-based iteration), no templates or RAII

gotchas: Keys that are a byte-for-byte prefix of another inserted key can cause out-of-bounds reads and incorrect behavior in recursive_insert (issue #56, open; related #12, #17, #54)

Path-compressed prefixes longer than MAX_PREFIX_LEN=10 bytes are only partially stored inline; matching a longer shared prefix requires re-reading a leaf key, a deliberate space/time tradeoff from the ART paper
Keys must already be binary-comparable byte strings; signed integers, floats, and multi-field keys need an explicit transform before insertion, the library does none of this for you
Leaf pointers are tagged in their low bit to distinguish them from internal nodes, so values/allocations the caller stores must not rely on odd pointer addresses
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libart only when you specifically need ordered + prefix iteration over binary-comparable byte-string keys and are willing to vendor and patch an abandoned C library. Every other sibling in this category (cpp-btree, tlx, frozenca/BTree, fast-containers, RadixMap, S+ tree, boost::container flat_set) has actual project-measured benchmarks against std::map; libart has none of its own, so prefer those when maintained, verifiable numbers matter more than ART's specific prefix/min/max feature set.
verified_claims_summary: The claimed speedups (up to ~14-17x on dense keys, ~5-10x on sparse keys at 65K-256M random 32-bit keys) are entirely from the ART paper (Leis et al., ICDE 2013), which benchmarked the paper authors' own unreleased ART and red-black-tree implementations, compiled with GCC 4.6 on an Intel Core i7-3930K (6C/12T, 3.2GHz, 12MB shared L3, 32GB DDR3-1600, Linux 3.2 x86-64) — not libart, and not any std::map implementation. libart itself has no benchmark suite.
status_note: Abandoned since its last commit on 2021-02-11; several confirmed bugs, including an unresolved out-of-bounds read for prefix-key inserts (#56), remain open years later. BSD-3-Clause and small enough (two files, src/art.c + src/art.h) to vendor and patch yourself if you accept that risk.
